title: How to turn one product photo into 10 campaign creatives

slides.head: One photo. Ten ways to sell the same product.
slides.body: You do not need a new photoshoot every time you want to promote something.

slides.head: Start with a clean product photo
slides.body: Use a clear image with the label and packaging visible. Keep this as your product reference.

slides.head: Ask AI for 10 directions
slides.body: Try: "Suggest 10 ad concepts for this body lotion. Include a setting, mood, customer, and headline for each."

slides.head: Choose 3 that suit your customers
slides.body: For example: bathroom shelf, morning routine, and gift box. More ideas are not always better ideas.

slides.head: Generate and check each creative
slides.body: Keep the original packaging accurate. Check labels, spelling, product shape, and claims before posting.

slides.head: Make each image do a job
slides.body: Use one to introduce the product, another to show a use case, and another to promote an offer.

slides.head: Try it with one product this week
slides.body: Save this workflow and tag @leverageaistudio when you try it.

title: Plan 30 days of marketing content with AI

slides.head: Posting every day is not a marketing plan.
slides.body: Start with what you want the content to achieve.

slides.head: Give AI the business context
slides.body: Share your product, price range, audience, most common customer question, and monthly goal.

slides.head: Ask for four weekly themes
slides.body: Example: problem awareness, product education, proof, and purchase decisions.

slides.head: Turn themes into specific posts
slides.body: Request 12 reels, 8 carousels and 10 stories. Ask for the message and next action for each.

slides.head: Make it sound like your business
slides.body: Replace generic phrases with what customers actually say. Add your offers, prices, and examples.

slides.head: Batch the work
slides.body: Write scripts first, create assets next, then schedule. Review performance at the end of each week.

slides.head: Start with this prompt
slides.body: "Build a 30-day plan for [business] targeting [customer] with a goal of [goal]. Make every post practical."

title: Create a product video ad without a studio

slides.head: Your product ad can start on your desk.
slides.body: A simple photo can become the starting point for a short video campaign.

slides.head: Decide on one message
slides.body: Example: "Make your room feel welcoming after a long day." Avoid trying to say everything.

slides.head: Write a 15-second script
slides.body: 0–3s: hook. 4–10s: product experience. 11–15s: product name and call to action.

slides.head: Build three visual shots
slides.body: A product close-up, an in-use scene, and a final branded product shot.

slides.head: Animate carefully
slides.body: Use subtle camera movement. Check that the AI does not change the label, cap, or packaging.

slides.head: Add the finishing touches
slides.body: Use readable captions, music you have rights to, and a simple "Shop now" or "Send us a message."

slides.head: Before you publish
slides.body: Watch without sound. Can someone still understand the offer? Save this checklist.

title: Build a launch campaign for a new product

slides.head: A launch should not be one "We are live" post.
slides.body: Give people a reason to notice the product before launch day.

slides.head: Seven days before: create curiosity
slides.body: Share the problem the product solves, behind-the-scenes work, or a partial reveal.

slides.head: Four days before: explain the product
slides.body: Show the features, how it is used, and who it is for.

slides.head: Two days before: answer objections
slides.body: Cover price, delivery areas, availability, and questions customers are likely to ask.

slides.head: Launch day: make buying simple
slides.body: Use one main offer, clear photos, working checkout links, and a direct call to action.

slides.head: After launch: keep talking
slides.body: Share FAQs, feedback, demonstrations, and reminders rather than disappearing.

slides.head: AI can help you organise it
slides.body: Ask for a seven-day timeline, then check and personalise every claim and detail.

title: Create five ad angles for the same product

slides.head: Same product. Different reasons people buy.
slides.body: One caption cannot speak to every customer need.

slides.head: Angle 1: solve a problem
slides.body: Example for bedsheets: "Tired of waking up on rough fabric?"

slides.head: Angle 2: show the experience
slides.body: Focus on what a restful, comfortable bedroom feels like.

slides.head: Angle 3: demonstrate the use
slides.body: Show how the product looks on an actual bed, not just in packaging.

slides.head: Angle 4: use proof
slides.body: Share genuine customer feedback, with permission. Do not invent testimonials.

slides.head: Angle 5: make the offer clear
slides.body: Explain available sizes, prices, delivery and how to order.

slides.head: Test the angles
slides.body: Change one message at a time. Compare enquiries, clicks and sales—not just likes.

title: Create a small-budget campaign for a local business

slides.head: You do not need a huge budget to run a thoughtful campaign.
slides.body: You need a clear customer, a clear offer, and useful content.

slides.head: Pick one product to promote
slides.body: Choose something customers understand and that you can fulfil reliably.

slides.head: Use what you already have
slides.body: A phone photo, customer questions, short demonstrations and existing reviews are enough to start.

slides.head: Ask AI to build your message
slides.body: Request three hooks, a 20-second video script and five captions for that one product.

slides.head: Create only the assets you need
slides.body: One video, one carousel and three story slides are a reasonable first campaign.

slides.head: Track actual responses
slides.body: Record messages, orders and costs in a simple sheet. Learn before spending more.

slides.head: Small campaign, clear result
slides.body: Start with one week and improve what is working.

title: How to Keep AI-generated brand visuals consistent

slides.head: Ever notice your AI product looks different in every image?
slides.body: That makes a brand feel less trustworthy.

slides.head: Create a short visual guide
slides.body: Record your colors, logo rules, product dimensions, packaging and preferred photography style.

slides.head: Use a reference image
slides.body: Upload a real product photo whenever the tool permits. Ask AI not to redesign the packaging.

slides.head: Repeat the details that matter
slides.body: Mention the same lighting, lens feel, background palette and brand mood in each prompt.

slides.head: Check for mistakes
slides.body: Look closely at text, labels, logos, skin details, shadows and extra objects.

slides.head: Keep a reference folder
slides.body: Save approved examples and reusable prompts to make the next campaign quicker.

slides.head: Consistency is deliberate
slides.body: AI helps create options. You still decide what looks like your brand.

title: Turn customer questions into a campaign

slides.head: Your next content ideas may already be in your DMs.
slides.body: People are telling you what they want to know.

slides.head: Collect 10 real questions
slides.body: Look at comments, WhatsApp chats, sales calls and customer enquiries.

slides.head: Group similar questions
slides.body: For example: pricing, how it works, delivery, quality, and who it is suitable for.

slides.head: Ask AI to shape the answers
slides.body: "Turn these customer questions into five educational posts. Keep the answers clear and avoid exaggerated claims."

slides.head: Choose the right format
slides.body: Use a reel for demonstrations, a carousel for explanations, and stories for quick answers.

slides.head: End with the next step
slides.body: Tell people where to order, ask questions or see the full product details.

slides.head: Use real customer language
slides.body: Do not replace clear everyday wording with complicated marketing terms.

title: Plan an AI brand ambassador campaign

slides.head: An AI face alone is not a brand strategy.
slides.body: A consistent character needs a clear role in your campaign.

slides.head: Decide what the character does
slides.body: Will they explain your product, act in fictional scenes, or demonstrate a routine?

slides.head: Create a character guide
slides.body: Specify appearance, clothing style, voice, personality, and things the character must never claim.

slides.head: Plan three repeatable scenes
slides.body: Example: product introduction, common customer question, and short lifestyle story.

slides.head: Keep people informed
slides.body: Do not portray the character as a real customer or make up personal results.

slides.head: Review every video
slides.body: Check product accuracy, lip-sync, captions, and brand fit.

slides.head: Build trust, not confusion
slides.body: Use AI creatively while being transparent about synthetic people.

title: How to automatically save customer enquiries into Google Sheets

slides.head: Still copying enquiries into a notebook?
slides.body: A simple form can help you keep them in one place.

slides.head: Create your enquiry form
slides.body: Ask only what you need: name, contact, product or service, and message.

slides.head: Connect it to a spreadsheet
slides.body: Google Forms can save responses directly to a linked Google Sheet.

slides.head: Organise the columns
slides.body: Add enquiry date, source, status, assigned person and next follow-up date.

slides.head: Set up an alert if needed
slides.body: Use a supported automation tool to notify you when a new row arrives.

slides.head: Test with a fake enquiry
slides.body: Check that the details arrive correctly and that no one else can see private customer data.

slides.head: Now you have a basic lead tracker
slides.body: Start here before paying for a complex CRM.

title: Build a simple customer follow-up system

slides.head: Interested customers sometimes need a follow-up.
slides.body: The difficult part is remembering who to contact and when.

slides.head: Create three clear statuses
slides.body: New enquiry, waiting for response, and closed. Keep it simple.

slides.head: Add a next-action date
slides.body: Record when the next message should go out and what the customer asked about.

slides.head: Choose what can be automated
slides.body: Send yourself reminders or draft a follow-up message. Review it before sending.

slides.head: Write a human follow-up
slides.body: "Hi Ada, checking whether you still need help choosing a size. Happy to answer any questions."

slides.head: Respect customer preferences
slides.body: Do not send repeated unwanted messages. Include a way to opt out of promotional contact.

slides.head: Track what happens
slides.body: Mark replies and sales. The goal is better service, not more messages.

title: Automate appointment confirmations and reminders

slides.head: Double bookings and forgotten calls are avoidable.
slides.body: Your booking page can handle the routine admin.

slides.head: Choose a booking tool
slides.body: Set your available days, time zone, meeting length and buffer between appointments.

slides.head: Collect useful details upfront
slides.body: Ask what the customer wants to discuss, without requesting unnecessary personal information.

slides.head: Connect your calendar
slides.body: Block unavailable times so people cannot book the same slot twice.

slides.head: Enable confirmations and reminders
slides.body: Send the time, location or call link, and a clear rescheduling option.

slides.head: Make one test booking
slides.body: Check the email, date, timezone and cancellation flow yourself.

slides.head: Keep the personal touch
slides.body: Automation handles the logistics. You still show up prepared.

title: Create an invoice reminder workflow

slides.head: Following up on invoices should not depend on memory.
slides.body: A simple tracker can tell you what is due.

slides.head: Start with an invoice sheet
slides.body: Include invoice number, customer, amount, issue date, due date, status, and payment reference.

slides.head: Set a reminder schedule
slides.body: For example: one reminder before the due date and one polite check-in after it.

slides.head: Only message unpaid invoices
slides.body: Make payment status your condition. Do not chase someone whose payment has already cleared.

slides.head: Use a helpful message
slides.body: "Hello, a quick reminder that invoice 104 is due on Friday. Please let us know if you need a copy."

slides.head: Review exceptions manually
slides.body: Disputes, partial payments and failed transactions should go to a person.

slides.head: Make collections more organised
slides.body: The system supports your process; it does not replace judgement.

title: Build a basic CRM using free tools

slides.head: A CRM is simply a way to keep track of customer relationships.
slides.body: You can begin with a spreadsheet.

slides.head: Create one record per lead
slides.body: Name, business, contact permission, interest, source and last conversation.

slides.head: Choose a short pipeline
slides.body: New, contacted, interested, proposal sent, won or lost.

slides.head: Give every lead a next step
slides.body: Add a date and a specific action, such as "send product catalogue."

slides.head: Use AI for summaries, not guesses
slides.body: Ask it to summarise notes you provide. Never let it invent what a customer said.

slides.head: Add automations gradually
slides.body: Start with form capture and reminders before attempting complex integrations.

slides.head: A useful CRM gets updated
slides.body: Keep it small enough that you will actually use it.

title: Create a daily sales summary automatically

slides.head: How much did the business actually sell today?
slides.body: You should not have to count scattered messages every evening.

slides.head: Record each sale in one place
slides.body: Capture the date, product, quantity, total paid, payment status and any refund.

slides.head: Create a simple daily summary
slides.body: Calculate orders, total sales, refunds, and net sales for each date.

slides.head: Build an easy dashboard
slides.body: A spreadsheet pivot table or chart can show your best-selling products.

slides.head: Schedule a summary
slides.body: Use an automation tool to email the daily totals from verified records.

slides.head: Check for gaps
slides.body: Cash sales, duplicate entries and unpaid orders can distort your numbers.

slides.head: Let the report guide action
slides.body: Use it to spot stock needs and customer demand—not just to admire a dashboard.

title: Get low-stock alerts before items finish

slides.head: Finding out you are out of stock when someone orders is stressful.
slides.body: Set a simple warning before that happens.

slides.head: List your products and quantities
slides.body: Include each product variant, opening stock, received units and sold units.

slides.head: Calculate available stock
slides.body: Available stock = opening stock + new stock - units sold.

slides.head: Set a reorder point
slides.body: Choose the quantity at which you should start replenishing each item.

slides.head: Add a notification rule
slides.body: When available stock drops to or below the reorder point, alert the responsible person.

slides.head: Check real inventory
slides.body: Review damaged, returned and reserved items so the sheet matches the shelf.

slides.head: Start with your fastest sellers
slides.body: You can expand the system once the numbers are reliable.

title: Build an FAQ assistant without misleading customers

slides.head: A chatbot should answer what it knows—not make things up.
slides.body: That is the most important rule.

slides.head: Collect approved answers
slides.body: Write down verified prices, delivery areas, opening hours, return policy and product information.

slides.head: Put the answers in one knowledge base
slides.body: Use a structured document or help centre that the assistant can reference.

slides.head: Set boundaries
slides.body: Tell the assistant to say "I'm not sure" and refer customers to a human when information is missing.

slides.head: Test difficult questions
slides.body: Try outdated prices, unavailable items, complaints and questions outside your services.

slides.head: Add an escalation option
slides.body: Let customers reach a real person without starting their enquiry again.

slides.head: Review conversations responsibly
slides.body: Improve the knowledge base while protecting customer information.

title: Write better AI prompts for campaigns

slides.head: "Give me a catchy caption" is not enough context.
slides.body: A better prompt begins with a clearer brief.

slides.head: Tell AI what you sell
slides.body: Mention the product, price category and what makes it useful.

slides.head: Describe the customer
slides.body: Who is buying, what do they care about, and what questions do they ask?

slides.head: Explain the objective
slides.body: Do you want enquiries, product education, website visits or sales?

slides.head: Set the tone and format
slides.body: Example: "Write three Instagram hooks in simple Nigerian English. No exaggerated claims."

slides.head: Ask for options and revise
slides.body: Choose one direction, then improve the opening, proof and call to action.

slides.head: Save this prompt structure
slides.body: Product + audience + goal + tone + format + constraints.

title: Find the first 5 tasks your business should automate

slides.head: You do not need to automate everything.
slides.body: Begin with the work you repeat most often.

slides.head: Write down your daily tasks
slides.body: Think about enquiries, orders, booking, receipts, reports and stock updates.

slides.head: Look for repeating steps
slides.body: Which task follows the same process every time and uses information you already capture?

slides.head: Score each task
slides.body: Rate frequency, time spent, error risk and ease of setup from 1 to 5.

slides.head: Choose one low-risk starting point
slides.body: Examples: appointment reminders or saving website enquiries to a spreadsheet.

slides.head: Keep approvals where they matter
slides.body: Do not automate refunds, sensitive decisions or public claims without suitable checks.

slides.head: Measure the difference
slides.body: After two weeks, compare time saved, errors and customer experience.

title: Connect your form, spreadsheet and email alert

slides.head: Let's build one useful workflow from start to finish.
slides.body: A new enquiry comes in. Your sheet updates. You get notified.

slides.head: Step 1: create a form
slides.body: Ask for the customer's name, email, service interest and short message.

slides.head: Step 2: connect the spreadsheet
slides.body: Use the form integration or an automation platform to create a row for each response.

slides.head: Step 3: set the trigger
slides.body: Choose "new form response" or "new spreadsheet row," depending on the tool.

slides.head: Step 4: send an internal email
slides.body: Include the service requested and a link to the record. Avoid exposing sensitive data.

slides.head: Step 5: test and fix
slides.body: Submit a sample response. Check duplicates, missing fields and notification delivery.

slides.head: You have a working mini-system
slides.body: Build one reliable flow before adding five more.
